q-29885:
First, we apply the sum rule and get

$$
\int ({x}^{2/3}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{x})\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2/3}\,\text{d}x+\sqrt{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x
$$

Now, using the power rule in the first term, and taking out the coefficient in the second term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2/3}\,\text{d}x+\sqrt{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{2/3+1}}{\frac{2}{3}+1}+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\  & =\frac{3}{5}{x}^{5/3}+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-103593:
First, we apply the sum rule and get

$$
\int ({x}^{3/2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1})\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x
$$

Now, using the power rule in the first term, and taking out the coefficient in the second term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{3/2+1}}{\frac{3}{2}+1}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{x}^{5/2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-10871:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+x)=4x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=4(1)+1=5,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =-\frac{1}{5}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{1}{5}+3 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5} & =0 \\ x & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(16,0).$

q-103546:
Let $f(x)=\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =-2{x}^{-3/2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{{1}^{3}}}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ 2y-8 & =x-1 \\ x-2y & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q-p=-7-(-2)=-5.$

q-141527:
First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{y}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{11}{2}y+25
$$

Now, here's the trick. We *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{11}{2})}^{2},$ writing the constant term $25$ last:

$$
{{y}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{11}{2}y+{(\frac{11}{2})}^{2}}_{⏟}-{(\frac{11}{2})}^{2}+25
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(y+\frac{11}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{11}{2})}^{2}+25
$$

Finally, evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(y+\frac{11}{2})}^{2}-\frac{21}{4}.
$$

q-140410:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $-1.$ So, we take out a factor of $-1$ from the entire expression:

$$
-({y}^{2}-5y+5)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{y}^{2}-5y+5
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{5}{2}y+5
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{5}{2})}^{2},$ writing the constant term $5$ last:

$$
{{y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{5}{2}y+{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}}_{⏟}-{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}+5
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(y-\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}+5
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(y-\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-\frac{5}{4}.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{y}^{2}+5y-5 & =-({(y-\frac{5}{2})}^{2}-\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =\frac{5}{4}-{(y-\frac{5}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-140330:
We begin by completing the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}+7x+10
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{7}{2}x+10
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{7}{2})}^{2},$ writing the constant term $10$ last:

$$
{{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{7}{2}x+{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}}_{⏟}-{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+10
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+10
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}-({x}^{2}+7x+10) & =-({(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}) \\  & =-{(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+\frac{9}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}-{(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-52522:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $2.$ So, we take out a factor of $2$ from the entire expression:

$$
2({x}^{2}-2x+\frac{3}{2})
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{x}^{2}-2x+\frac{3}{2}
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x+\frac{3}{2}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${1}^{2},$ writing the constant term $\frac{3}{2}$ last:

$$
{{x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x+{1}^{2}}_{⏟}-{1}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
(x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
(x-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}2({x}^{2}-2x+\frac{3}{2}) & =2((x-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =2{(x-1)}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =2{(x-1)}^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

q-52537:

$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{6}x
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}:$ 

$$
{{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{6}x+{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}}_{⏟}-{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}
$$

$$
{(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}-\frac{1}{36}

$$
\begin{aligned}6({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}x) & =6({(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}-\frac{1}{36}) \\  & =6{(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}-6\cdot \frac{1}{36} \\  & =6{(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}-\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

q-35079:
Notice that the leading coefficient is $-2.$ So, we take out a factor of $-2$ from the entire expression:

$$
-2({z}^{2}+7z-8)
$$

Let's now complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
{z}^{2}+7z-8
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{7}{2}\cdot z-8
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{7}{2})}^{2},$ writing the constant term $8$ last:

$$
{{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{7}{2}\cdot z+{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}}_{⏟}-{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-8
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(z+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-8
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(z+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-\frac{81}{4}.
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression::

$$
\begin{aligned}-2({z}^{2}+7z-8) & =-2({(z+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-\frac{81}{4}) \\  & =-2{(z+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+(-2)\cdot (-\frac{81}{4}) \\  & =-2{(z+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+\frac{81}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-140378:

-9({z}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}z-1)
$$

$$
{z}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}z-1
$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{3}\cdot z-1
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{1}{3})}^{2},$ writing the constant term $1$ last:

$$
{{z}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{3}\cdot z+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}_{⏟}-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-1
$$

{(z+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-1

q-141817:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{y}^{2}-8y+16=(y-4)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2}-40y & =-76 \\ 5({y}^{2}-8y) & =-76 \\ 5({y}^{2}-2\cdot 4y) & =-76 \\ 5({y}^{2}-2\cdot 4y+{4}^{2}-{4}^{2}) & =-76 \\ 5[(y-4)^{2}-{4}^{2}] & =-76 \\ 5[(y-4)^{2}-16] & =-76 \\ 5(y-4)^{2}-80 & =-76\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $80$ to both sides and then dividing by $5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5(y-4)^{2}-80 & =-76 \\ 5(y-4)^{2}-80+80 & =-76+80 \\ 5(y-4)^{2} & =4 \\ (y-4)^{2} & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-4)^{2} & =\frac{4}{5} \\ \sqrt{(y-4)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{5}} \\ |y-4| & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ y-4 & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ y & =4\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

q-141811:
Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}+6x+9=(x+3)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+24x & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+6x) & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x) & =-11 \\ 4({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}) & =-11 \\ 4[(x+3)^{2}-{3}^{2}] & =-11 \\ 4[(x+3)^{2}-9] & =-11 \\ 4(x+3)^{2}-36 & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $36$ to both sides and then dividing by $4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x+3)^{2}-36 & =-11 \\ 4(x+3)^{2}-36+36 & =-11+36 \\ 4(x+3)^{2} & =25 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =\frac{25}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2} & =\frac{25}{4} \\ \sqrt{(x+3)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}} \\ |x+3| & =\frac{5}{2} \\ x+3 & =\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-3\pm \frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{11}{2},\,-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-112524:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+6x-5 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x) & =5 \\ 4[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}\cdot x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{16}] & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{9}{16} & =5 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =5 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{29}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{3}{4}$ and $q=\frac{29}{4}.$ Finally,

$$
p+q=\frac{3}{4}+\frac{29}{4}=\frac{32}{4}=8.
$$
